newsitem.title: FRANCE: French rivals feud over tv debate in tight race.
newsitem.headline: French rivals feud over tv debate in tight race.

text.p: French political leaders traded charges of cowardice on Friday over a television debate as the campaign for a snap parliamentary election looked increasingly risky for President Jacques Chirac's centre-right government.

Opposition Socialist leader Lionel Jospin, buoyed by a poll suggesting left and right are neck-and-neck, rejected a four-way debate with leaders of other parliamentary parties and challenged Prime Minister Alain Juppe to a one-on-one showdown.

Juppe, centre-right UDF party leader Francois Leotard and Communist leader Robert Hue all said they had accepted the private TF1 channel's invitation for a four-way debate on May 20, five days before the first round of voting.
But Jospin said on a campaign trip to Toulouse in southern France: "It is as if (Juppe) needed a second because he is scared of a direct confrontation with me.
"He prefers doubles but I play singles," said the Socialist leader, a keen tennis player. "The question remains: does Mr Juppe want to confront me or doesn't he?"
Two senior Juppe lieutenants -- Interior Minister Jean-Louis Debre and Gaullist party secretary-general Jean-Francois Mancel -- promptly accused Jospin of running scared.

The shadow-boxing reflected both the Socialists' drive to focus the campaign on Juppe's unpopular record and personality, and the ruling coalition's effort to depict Jospin as dependent on the Communists for a parliamentary majority.
A four-way debate would be likely to highlight differences between the Socialists and Communists on the key issue of a single European currency.
Hue said he was surprised and disappointed at Jospin's refusal. The two leaders are due to meet next Tuesday to adopt a declaration of intention to govern together if the left wins.

Further highlighting the conservatives' sensitivity to Juppe's unpopularity, Leotard said in a newspaper interview to be published on Saturday that Chirac had not decided whether to return Juppe as premier if the conservatives won the election.
He said Chirac had many centre-right politicians to choose from and that it was simplistic to think a new Juppe government was a foregone conclusion.

"The president is entirely free to choose," Leotard told daily Le Figaro. "By definition, the president of the republic will make his decision only after hearing what the people say on May 25 and June 1," he said.
Opinion pollsters said the election race seemed extremely tight and public opinion was very volatile.

An IPSOS opinion poll taken on Tuesday and Wednesday found the ruling coalition would win 292 seats in the 577-member National Assembly, just three more than the 289 required for a majority, with the opposition Socialists taking 256, the Communists 28 and the far-right National Front one.
"Statistically speaking, they (the majority and the Left) are level," Pierre Giacometti of IPSOS told Reuters.
Thirty-one percent of voters questioned did not state their voting intention, and almost 40 percent of those who did said they might still change their minds.
Giacometti said that according to his institute's model some 180 seats hung on a margin of less than five percentage points.
Rumours that polls yet to be published showed the left with a slight lead caused the franc, interest rate futures and shares to fall on French financial markets on Friday, dealers said.

Taking to the hustings for the first time since President Chirac dissolved parliament on Monday, Juppe accused the Socialists on Thursday night of betraying their European ideals and planning archaic tax-and-spend policies.

"The Socialists, powerfully aided by their Communist allies, without whose votes they have no hope of a majority, have got the wrong century," Juppe told a rally in Marseille. "You wonder whether they see the world as it is."
Speaking at the same rally, Leotard also played up the theme of the "Socialo-Communist" threat which dominated French election campaigns of the 1970s and 1980s.
"Every time Mr Jospin depicts us as harsh capitalists, we will call them the Marxists they really are," he said.

Partly in an attempt to forge an electoral pact with the Communists, who he is due to meet next Tuesday, Jospin has posed conditions for a single European currency, ruling out further austerity to prepare for the euro.
